opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today’s readings left me with questions because they seem to begin with certainty and end by stretching that certainty into something larger.

In 2 Timothy, Paul speaks about sacred Scripture almost like he is handing us a map before departing. Scripture is not presented merely as information or moral advice, but as something that teaches, corrects, trains, and equips us. The goal does not seem to be simply collecting knowledge, but allowing ourselves to be shaped by it. This may be part of why we are given time at all — to be refined, corrected, strengthened, and slowly formed into people capable of greater good. Closeness to God is not found by accidentally wandering into Him, but by repeatedly entering His word until it begins shaping the course beneath our feet.

Psalm 119 continues this movement. There is peace for those who love His law. There is permanence in His words. “All my ways are before you.” Life often feels less like a straight line and more like wandering while trying to remain on course, trusting that even when we meander, our path still remains before God. Scripture equips us, God sees us, and we stay close to His word and find peace there.

Then Mark interrupts everything. Jesus asks, “How do the scribes claim that the Christ is the son of David?” Then He quotes David himself: “The Lord said to my lord, sit at my right hand until I place your enemies under your feet.” At first, this sounds like a contradiction, but it is expansion. Jesus is not denying that the Messiah comes from David’s line. He is asking how David can call his own descendant “Lord.”

This is the point. Jesus is forcing them to confront that the Messiah is greater than expected. Not merely political, not merely human, not merely another king. David’s son, yes — but also David’s Lord.

This is how the readings connect. Scripture equips the journey. The Psalms remind us God sees the journey. Then Jesus asks the deeper question: do you truly know who walks beside you on that journey?

Today’s readings first give confidence in the road, only to ask whether we understand who stands both at the destination and beside us while we walk it.
